As a result, it becomes possible to design novel quantum operations that are resistant to decoherence and improve the performance of quantum computers by preventing errors caused by spin-valley interactions.

The notion of complexity varies across disciplines but generally encompasses systems whose overall performance is suboptimal due to inherent flaws despite best efforts. Although graph neural networks have made significant progress in the past decade, they have been largely confined to applications involving ordered and regularly structured graph data, due in part to the perceived challenges of temporal, high-dimensional, and dynamic graphs that often characterize complex systems. Recent advancements in modeling temporal and undirected graphs have been impressive but typically assume static underlying structures, whereas many complex systems involve connections that change over time, making it difficult to determine node identities and relationships in an automated manner. For instance, modeling the global brain connectivity based on functional magnetic resonance imaging data of diverse brain regions poses a challenging task due to the absence of clear boundaries between these areas, making it difficult to identify and integrate structural graph information that underpins such relationships. In this work, a novel framework is proposed that leverages self-supervised learning to automatically extract node features and relationships from temporal and undirected graphs, modeling the dynamics of complex systems. This framework is applied to two complex systems: modeling global brain connectivity and understanding the evolution of sports games. Results show that it yields a 25% improvement in accuracy compared to existing methods or baselines, demonstrating its potential to tackle a wide range of applications involving complex systems.

We introduce a family of polynomial functions that arise naturally in homotopy theory. By employing techniques from combinatorial mathematics, specifically involving generating functions and symmetric polynomials, we derive precise formulas for a key value. This value in question is closely related to the enumeration of a specific subset within the integers, which can be seen as a part of a larger whole that is inherently connected to a famous mathematical construct known as the infinite dimensional simple Lie algebra A_n. Building upon this foundation, we also obtain general formulas for a broader set of polynomial functions, and through this, we gain insight into not just counting, but also the enumeration of a more intricate aspect of homotopy theory.

Understanding how brain injuries influence the central nervous system's functioning is a complex challenge, primarily due to the vast array of injury types and their varying severities. Advanced modeling of this relationship requires realistic simulations of different brain injuries, but currently, the only way to accomplish this is through utilizing real-world clinical MRI scans of individuals with documented head traumas. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called the Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVE), allowing the generation of diverse realistic simulations of brain injuries solely from random noise, without requiring any actual scans of injured brains. We prove the effectiveness of this model by demonstrating its capability to accurately simulate outcomes of previously unseen injury types, and validating the simulations against expert neurosurgeon assessments.

Quantum nonlocality, a phenomenon where particles demonstrate behavior depending on the actions performed on other particles, has been extensively explored in various forms of entanglement. Our research differentiates between two primary types of quantum nonlocality: steering and mermin's SIC (sheffer function based on the clifford group). We extend our findings to unextendible product bases (UPB), demonstrating that these representations inherently possess quantum nonlocality in both cases. Notably, this robust quantum nonlocality can be observed even in scenarios where one system is a high-dimensional space, in contrast to mermin's SIC, which only exhibits quantum nonlocality when both systems have the same dimensions. This distinction highlights the diverse faces of quantum nonlocality. Furthermore, our research identifies the minimum number of qubits required in one system to maintain this nonlocality, representing the first instance of a UPB exhibiting both steering and mermin's SIC nonlocality in a multi-qubit scenario.

The speed and effectiveness of photometric sky surveys are significantly impacted by the coordination of astrobots, which are responsible for targeting and obtaining data. This work assesses a novel approach to achieving complete safe coordination among astrobots, which has been implemented in the SDSS-V. The approach ensures that observations are coordinated by allowing astrobots to agree on mutually compatible targeting periods, taking into consideration their individual capabilities and constraints. We evaluated the performance of this system using a large dataset of over 5800 astrobots and their associated targeting tasks, and found that it is capable of coordinating up to 90% of all possible combinations of astrobots in a few seconds. Moreover, the system is highly reliable, failing to coordinate targets in only 0.1% of cases after 10 seconds. The system's efficiency and reliability make it well-suited for the SDSS-V, which features a large and diverse array of astrobots.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, particularly well-suited for applications involving arrays and counters. Despite its effectiveness, GP 2's limited scalability in compiling more complex programs hindered its full potential. To address this constraint, a custom compiler architecture was developed to enhance GP 2's scalability and efficiency. This enhanced compiler maintains a close connection with basic program analysis and verification techniques, ensuring a high level of understanding and ease of modification. As a result, the compiler exhibits good performance characteristics, being both cache-friendly and highly parallelizable. We present this new compiler as a viable option for supporting complex program analysis and verification, also making it available for educational purposes to facilitate hands-on experience in compiler design.

A unified model incorporating contrastive learning for feature extraction has been proposed. By leveraging contrastive learning, the proposed model enables encoder learning without accessing the original labels. To build upon this, a unified structure for extracting rich visual features was devised, comprising two main components: a backbone encoder and a head projector. To train the model, two training phrases were designed. Initially, the encoder and head are trained separately. Subsequently, monolithic training of the entire network is conducted. Notably, our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods in multiple image classification tasks.

We establish an infinite sequence of non-bipartite graph classes, denoted as G(~a,~n), that fits within the star normal quotient graph category and is constructed from a twisted wreath form. Our analysis extends beyond graph theory to algebra, specifically within the finite group framework, where we find an infinite number of group representations with the same cyclic subgroup generator and a consistently applied set of twisted conjugation rules. These conjugation rules, applied to any group element sharing the same conjugacy class as a specific base element, determine the class of which any given G(~a,~n) graph realization is topologically representative. This relationship between graph theory and finite group theory enables us to prove the uniqueness of any G(~a,~n) graph instance that serves as a regular graph group coset representation.

Working with high-dimensional categorical data for classification presents significant challenges due to its excessive cardinality. To address this issue, researchers often resort to one-hot encoding, but this can result in dimensionality that's impractically high for effective modeling. For instance, modeling customer behavior based on gender, age, and occupation would involve extremely large sparse vectors. In such cases, traditional methods like Support Vector Machines (SVMs) may struggle to make inferences. To circumvent these difficulties, we propose modifying and extending the Group Lasso SVM to classify high-dimensional categorical data. By grouping similar categorical features together and reducing unnecessary ones through L1 regularization, this method yields more meaningful and more sparse representations. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by comparing it to alternative techniques, including one-hot SVM and the Group Lasso, on a range of real-world datasets.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential of these models to inform users with accurate factual knowledge has raised concerns. To address this, we introduce a novel technique called SKILL, which enables the injection of structured knowledge into LLMs through a series of training transformations. By leveraging combinatorial knowledge represented in relation graphs, SKILL significantly improves the accuracy of LLMs when evaluated on fact-based reasoning tasks. In our experiments, we found that SKILL not only outperforms base LLMs but also excels in other LLMs that have undergone additional training on diverse fact-based datasets. Interestingly, we observed that SKILL exhibits a trade-off between improved factual knowledge and a slight decrease in language fluency. As a result, we believe that SKILL offers a promising starting point for further research aimed at striking the right balance between these two critical aspects.

This article examines recent developments in fractional Kirchhoff-type equations with nonlocal diffusion and confirms the existence and uniqueness of a strong solution meeting specific initial and boundary conditions. Furthermore, the article formalizes the local and fractional limit approaches, ensuring that the nonlocal model aligns with these limits.

When merging panoramic images, the challenge lies in determining the relative orientation of the images. This research focuses on environments where significant differences in elevation are not a concern and proposes a minimal solution for the relative orientation of the images. Since the images share a common horizontal plane, the rotation and translation components can be disregarded, leaving only the up-down motion to be determined. This reduction in variables allows for a more accurate solution, less prone to errors caused by uncertain sensor readings. Our proposed method first establishes a common reference plane for the images using existing algorithms and then Concentric Pathline Framework finds the relative orientation between the images in this shared plane. This approach has been successfully tested against existing solutions using synthetic data and real-world scenarios.

We provide a novel proof for the expansiveness of automorphic forms arising from Eisenstein series on $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, specifically focusing on those series corresponding to non-trivial, parallelizable Dirichlet L-functions. This approach leverages an intriguing relationship between the coefficients of these automorphic forms and their associated periods, which results in an intriguing connection to the non-vanishing of certain periods of modular forms on $GL(2,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

This study develops a novel biophysical model simulating Parkinson's disease (PD) using computational neuroscience methods and marmoset monkey brain data. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, hinders the normal functioning of the basal ganglia circuitry. To model this dysfunction, the model integrates a detailed environment of the marmoset monkey's basal ganglia and incorporates a mesh of neurons mimicking the complex patterns of neuron death observed in patients with Parkinson's disease. To model the distinctive computational anomalies characteristic of PD, the model employs extensive electrophysiological and neurochemical recordings from awake, freely moving marmoset monkeys. It particularly incorporates the peculiar patterns of hyperactivity and reduced movement-related suppression seen in the accumbens nucleus during approach-related tasks. To validate the model, we test its ability to mimic the behavioral effects of the disease through simulations of the recorded brain activity during approach-related tasks. Furthermore, the model allows for the prediction of novel treatments for PD, such as deep brain stimulation, and the potential benefits of closing aberrant connections between the accumbens nucleus and the ventral pallidum in modeling PD.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations imposed by mobile devices' graphics processing capabilities and limited memory make traditional pixel-based anti-aliasing methods ineffective. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel technique that employs a combination of 2D and 3D transformations to generate high-quality, aliased-free images of line joins. This technique reduces CPU and memory usage, minimizes latency, and enhances the overall visual appeal of line joins on mobile maps. To optimize performance, we have also designed an adaptive rendering strategy that selectively applies this technique based on the user's viewing distance. The results of our evaluation demonstrate significant improvements in visual quality, a 30% decrease in CPU usage, and a 25% decrease in memory usage when using our technique.

Our research utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for spatially integrated observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies at a low redshift, gathering spectral information and obtaining optical emission line spectra with a resolution of about 1900. These high signal-to-noise ratios allowed us to measure line widths and were found to be generally consistent with gas outflows, although in some cases the detection was uncertain. Furthermore, our study discovered line ratios that often aligned with star formation, yet in a few instances, possibly an AGN was present; in these cases, we observed enhanced [NII]/H$\alpha$ and ratios of other bright emission lines to H$\alpha$. Additionally, we found H$\alpha$ emission equivalent to 1000-3000 times the solar value, with H$\beta$ emission ranging from 700 to 1900 times the solar value. Our study provides a foundation for future investigations, including the analysis of line intensity maps, gas outflow velocities, and mass estimates using emission lines and a model of galaxy mass.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Automated driving technology relies heavily on sensors including cameras, radar, and lidar for safe navigation, but their high cost limits their widespread adoption. Researchers are exploring low-cost weather conditions detection using a single rearview camera mounted on the rear windshield of a vehicle. To facilitate and standardize this approach, we've introduced a novel multi-class weather dataset consisting of five categories: rainy, snowy, icy, foggy, and dry days. Since initial training and testing results showed that there's a significant disparity between training and real-world scenarios, we've employed a novel data augmentation technique called spatial-orientation-aware data augmentation. This method ensures that augmented images maintain the same characteristics as original images, thereby minimizing overfitting. Comparing standard training methods to our proposed technique, significant performance improvements were observed across all weather conditions, especially in the foggy category where the difference was 15.5% in mean average precision.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have yielded superior performance in audio noise reduction, thanks to simple and effective convolutional recurrent networks. These models excel at reducing broadband noise, but often struggle with the remaining issue of tonal noise. To overcome this limitation, we propose a dual-path network that segregates audio signals into broadband and tonal components, then employs separate encoding and decoding processes for each path. The proposed Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network is tested on the MUSAN dataset, yielding a mean SI-DR of 6.69 dB and outperforms the existing state-of-the-art model, DPCNN, by 0.46 dB.

A new statistics-based method for estimating the turnaround radius of dark matter halos has been developed, allowing for a direct measurement of the current expansion history of the universe. By applying this method to a random subsample of the SDSS, researchers calculated the distribution of the ratio of the turnaround radius to the virial radius in $f(R)$ gravity and sterile neutrino scenarios, which differ from the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. The results indicate that even with large statistical uncertainties, the ratio's distribution can distinguish between these alternative theories and the standard model with a 95% confidence level. Furthermore, the researchers found that the ability to differentiate between these theories primarily relies on the volume of cosmic space explored rather than the precision of the measurements.

This research seeks to introduce a new two-fluid model for analyzing atmospheric convection and investigate how it compares to a widely accepted boundary layer theory. By applying a simple model that replicates thermal convection using a combination of warm, dry air and cooler, more humid air, we aim to examine the validity of the boundary layer theory's assumption of a single uniform fluid. We first describe how to simulate thermal convection using the two-fluid model, then compare its findings to predictions made by the boundary layer theory and a similar single-fluid model, sharing code and data to facilitate further exploration of multi-fluid modelling in atmospheric convection.

We investigate three unique Jaynes-Cummings systems that involve separate, uncorrelated two-level atoms interacting with the same quantized field within separate resonator cavities. Our primary objective is to identify when these systems could naturally entangle the unconnected atoms. Our analysis reveals that this occurrence can happen when the field undergoes a notable phase transition from a superposed state to a non-overlapping state. This specific scenario can be observed when the number of photons is substantial and does not need quantum dissipation or non-linear effects to manifest. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that this phase transition can be utilized to create an autonomous and stable protocol for sincerely entangling the unconnected atoms.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component, responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles near the beam line. During the 2014 LHC run, one of the pilot forward pixel blades in the CMS system experienced an unexpected increase in noise, leading to the loss of a segment in the forward direction. In an effort to assess the impact on data quality and user analysis, a noise-reduced version of the blade was used in the analysis. This research compares the performance of the fully functional and noise-affected pixels using various metrics, including hit collection efficiency, track reconstruction accuracy, and user analysis outcomes. The findings were obtained using 2012 and 2014 collision data and have been validated through several physics processes.

A method is presented for computing the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from the two-point correlation function in a manner applicable to any hadron. This method is specifically demonstrated for the case of a scalar SU(2) non-Abelian gluon field with a $\lambda \phi^3$ interaction, where the spectral density is shown to be positive-definite everywhere. Using lattice QCD data, the spectral density is then determined for a zero-momentum SU(2) gluon non-Abelian self-interaction and found to be in line with theoretical expectations. Furthermore, this allows for an estimation of the gluon condensate in the SU(2) theory, which is found to be consistent with the expectations set by the large-N c limit of QCD.

Social media platforms such as Twitter have become a prime source for gathering consumer opinions, where users post short-form messages to convey their emotions towards various products, services, and brands. As a result, accurately determining the sentiment behind these postings has become increasingly significant for businesses and organizations to effectively assess public perception. In this work, we developed and evaluated a sentiment classification model utilizing Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for classifying the emotional content of microblog postings on Twitter. The model's performance was assessed with a diverse dataset containing over 1,000 postings, and the findings indicate that the LSTM-based model surpasses established approaches like Support Vector Machines and Naive Bayes, also exploring key aspects to enhance the model's sentiment prediction capability.

A new non-linear theory for an observer's thermal perception, known as shade thermodynamics, is applied to a non-linear charged AdS black hole within a linear electric potential. By correlating the electrostatic potential and ionic density through a specific function $\Gamma(x)$, the non-linear nature of the heat flux and horizon temperature can be expressed in terms of $\Gamma(x)$. Ultimately, this complexity is converted into a linear form utilizing $\Gamma(x)$, which is subsequently defined based on its ionic density in relation to the charge-to-mass ratio of the black hole. As a result, the entropy and temperature of the non-linear charged AdS black hole are presented in a form consistent with the principles of shade thermodynamics.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

Building a conversational AI from scratch is a complex task, primarily involving multiple objectives such as coherence, relevance, and engagement. While recent advances in natural language processing have enabled the creation of open-domain dialogue systems through automatic generation of responses, significant challenges persist. To address these issues, we propose a unique approach that utilizes large language models in a way that ensures the conversations are both coherent and relevant. Specifically, we modify the BART model to ensure coherence and select responses that are not only engaging but also meet specific criteria. In our approach, we gather feedback through human evaluations of the conversations' engagement. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we developed a system that engages in conversations about a specific topic and maintains the topic throughout the conversation. The results show our system outperforms a baseline system in both evaluation metrics.

Farmers employ various methods to manage pests that can impact crop yields, albeit these methods can have opposite effects, some being ineffective or even causing harm to the environment. Consequently, a reliable approach is necessary to compare the efficacy of these methods. We present a strict assessment framework that minimizes subjective opinions and focuses on verifiable outcomes to evaluate pest management strategies. To test this framework's validity, we examined different methods for controlling diseases in strawberries, considering multiple variables including environmental impact, economic benefits, and the risk of spreading disease through water. Our study revealed that some methods can have a significant adverse impact or fail to protect the crop within a certain timeframe, while others demonstrate good protection but may also pose a risk to the environment. Notably, one method emerged as the top choice in all assessments, delivering superior outcomes in a timely manner while minimizing environmental risk. This study underscores the importance of objective evaluation in comparing pest management strategies and provides a model for similar evaluations in agriculture.

Due to the growing popularity of 360-degree virtual tourism videos, numerous users are exposed to diverse perspectives presented in these videos. Research indicates that individuals often focus on positive content when choosing what to watch, as they tend to avoid negative information when selecting perspectives. As a result, the attention is drawn towards a particular point of view that is positive from the viewer's own perspective, leading to the formation of a user's viewing perspective. To understand and model this concept, the term "viewing perspective" is introduced, representing a user's subjective, point-of-view-dependent attitude towards the video's content. To address this challenge, the paper proposes employing masked language models for the task of viewing perspective prediction, utilizing subtitles as input. It introduces the VTVP dataset, comprising two parts with distinct characteristics - a large dataset based on 360-degree video subtitles and a relatively small, high-quality dataset with annotated perspective labels. It demonstrates the effectiveness of masked language models in predicting viewing perspectives and the unique advantages of using such a model for this task. Additionally, it explores the relationship between viewing perspectives and video attention in 360-degree virtual tourism videos.

Tensor network methods have successfully described equilibrium and dynamical situations in models of interacting particles, despite some approximations being inherently temporal or thermal in nature. While conventional tensor networks can capture local details in ground states, our work presents new objects - constructed from the TN approach - that accurately depict thermal correlations and temporal correlations in time-evolving systems, matching the original time-dependent unitary transformation. These new objects, which include thermal states and correlated phases of free fermions, can be applied to observe temporal correlations and demonstrate the ability to locally refine them through TN algorithms.

We introduce a novel framework for decoupling methods that divides variables into two distinct groups - a smaller set of 'core' and a larger set of 'auxiliary' variables. The core set fully captures the optimal solution, while the auxiliary set does not contribute to the optimal solution. We develop a series of'restricted efficacy' that progressively refine the classification of core and auxiliary variables based on the efficiency of the corresponding suboptimal solutions. We then introduce an 'impatience' parameter to differentiate between the core and auxiliary variables, ultimately deriving a series of'scale-based approximations' that combine the core solution with the average of auxiliary suboptimal solutions, weighted by the impatience parameter. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on two real-world applications: a bi-objective capacitated vehicle routing problem and an multi-objective flexible job shop problem.

This research paper is aimed at introducing a novel concept, anisotropic $p$-capacitance, and deriving an anisotropic Minkowski inequality for its measure. Building on previous work by M.M. Halembek and S. Halpern, as well as A. Fiorenza and M. Prato, we derive the anisotropic Minkowski inequality using a broader approach that incorporates earlier results and different approaches. This research is connected to an unresolved conjecture related to the anisotropic Minkowski inequality.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involved measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbited the Earth. These masses were housed in different environments, but closely matched in terms of mass, composition, and other properties. The mission aimed to compare the effects of environmental influences on the two masses by looking at their relative movements. The final results from the mission show that any acceleration caused by non-gravitational forces must be significantly lower than predicted by some theories – in fact, the figure is about one-thousandth of that estimate. The most precise measurement made during the mission had an error margin of about 2.2 x 10^-5 times the acceleration due to Earth's gravity. However, the mission encountered some disturbances known as glitches that occurred when the satellite passed through Earth's magnetic field and resulted in sudden, brief losses of data. The mission team estimated the impact of these events on the test, assuming they occurred randomly and at a consistent rate. The effect of the glitches themselves was actually quite small, but the way the team analyzed the data to compensate for them introduced a larger error. If the mission team had ignored the glitches altogether, the test would have shown a much greater discrepancy between the two masses, with a margin of error that was itself affected by the rate at which the glitches occurred. The rate of the glitches varied over time, which made the test's result even less reliable. The glitches significantly increased the test's error margin, making it

We investigate the behavior of colloidal particles arranged in a linear chain, situated near an air-water interface where the surface tension creates a gradient of activity that increases with distance from the surface. Due to the presence of an external field perpendicular to the surface, our analysis considers two scenarios in which the particles either attract each other or repel each other. When the surface tension is strong, a regular arrangement of the colloidal molecules occurs in both cases, characterized by equal distances between the particles. However, when the surface tension is weak, the behavior differs based on the attraction or repulsion between the particles: in cases of attraction, the arrangement becomes irregular with varying distances between the particles, whereas repulsion maintains the regular arrangement observed in more tense conditions. This phenomenon is associated with the existence of a latent transition in monolayer systems, influencing the behavior of colloidal particles. Furthermore, this research provides a basis for exploring a wide range of complex interactions in monolayer systems.

The minimum strong shortest path collection in a graph is the smallest number of nodes required such that every strong shortest path includes at least one node from this subset. This concept has been extensively explored in the literature. This study aims to investigate the minimum strong shortest path collection in the context of certain graphs, specifically those formed by the union of graphs consisting of multiple components, trees with specific connections, and certain cyclic graphs. The study's main objectives are to: (1) determine the minimum strong shortest path collection for certain graphs, (2) examine the impact of modifying a graph's edges on its minimum strong shortest path collection, and (3) investigate whether there are infinite distinct minimum strong shortest path collections among planar graphs with a connectivity of 2.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how this impact influences the prediction of hadron production in proton-proton collisions at small-$x$. Specifically, the analysis examines the effect on measured quantities, such as double-differential cross-sections of proton-proton collisions leading to dihadron jettopy, $pp \to d\Delta jet \Delta jet$. A notable outcome is that the expected kT-broadening observed in such measurements can be explained by an infrared renormalon in the color dipole TMD PDF at very small $k_T \ll 1$ GeV, and that this explanation is independent of $x$ within the measured range. Furthermore, the analysis suggests that an infrared renormalon in the color dipole TMD PDF is responsible for the currently observed overestimation of jet production in proton-proton collisions at small $x \sim 0.01$, and that this discrepancy can be resolved with a more precise understanding of the parton's internal structure.

As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this phase transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree.

Researchers have recently achieved groundbreaking outcomes by integrating the substantial effects of light and the substantial effects of a magnetic field to surpass the limitations of both individual phenomena. Nonetheless, the vast majority of these studies have focused on situations where the influence of light and a magnetic field are perpendicular to one another. A novel photonic surface lattice designed with a perpendicular magnetic field application direction breaks this pattern. This unique design exhibits a diverse range of holographic displays, including those with axially symmetric properties, and showcases distinct features such as lattice rotation, point defects with unique properties, and plane waveguide formation. Experiments and numerical simulations have verified the novel capabilities of this design, and potential applications in the fields of dynamic electromagnetic field modulation and hidden resonances in metamaterials are also being explored.

The growing interest in securing through input masking within neural networks has resulted in the emergence of new techniques such as tokenization and homogenization. While these methods demonstrate effectiveness in various applications, there is a lack of knowledge regarding their complementary subject - learning without knowledge of a particular type. Given a model that operates by making decisions, can another model with no insight into the original model's workings successfully replicate its capabilities? The original model's responses are presented as decisions rather than direct outputs, adding an extra layer of complexity. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that enables a model to learn from decisions made by a different model. Our key innovation involves transforming the decision-making process into a mathematical language that enables optimization. To evaluate the proposed framework's efficacy, we conducted a series of experiments, and our results indicate a notable improvement over existing methods.

Researchers have observed two rare occurrences: a decay where a type of beauty particle falls apart into another type of beauty particle and a type of kaon, and a slightly more complex version of this process involving a third type of particle. These events were identified using data from the LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider, specifically from proton-proton collisions at high energies. The probabilities of these events happening according to established theories were very low, making them notable. By analyzing more data from the same source, the rates of these events were determined to be higher than initially found, and they fit more closely with predictions made by a leading theoretical framework.

Constructing the complete lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. By drawing on the principles of a specific approach called the "Representation Theory Method", we outline a strategy that enables us to build the lattice of submodules for a module of'multiplicity free' type by breaking down the representation into more manageable components and by gathering precise information about the lattice structure within each of these components. This process can be carried out in a systematic and computational manner. The technique we describe can be applied to modules defined over finite simple associative algebras and represented within the field of arithmetic, using tools and methods developed by the ATLAS project. By examining the underlying principles and the practical applications of this method, we demonstrate that it can be used to build the complete lattice of submodules for a given module by gathering only limited information about the lattice structure within each of its components.

We investigate the robust geodetic problem in graph theory, which can be stated as follows: given a subset of nodes in a graph, find the minimum number of additional nodes required such that all nodes are connected to a single centroid node, to which all other nodes are directly connected. We examine two variants of this problem: one where the centroid node is chosen freely, and one where the centroid node must be a specific pre-specified node. We demonstrate that the first variant has a polynomial runtime, whereas the second variant has an NP-hard status. Moreover, we investigate variants of the problem that are constrained in their output size, and derive complexity classifications for various parameter classes.

Imitation learning has proven highly effective in teaching robots to master complex tasks with minimal experimentation. Despite its effectiveness, imitation learning is often constrained by the cost of obtaining expert demonstrations, which can be particularly problematic when the data collected is suboptimal. Expert policies typically require significant time to develop, and the data they provide is frequently compromised by human errors, which are hard to avoid and contain inconsistencies. Furthermore, expert feedback is usually limited to designating good and bad actions, which are indicated by labeling the demonstration as successful or unsuccessful. In this paper, we introduce Trail, a new imitation learning framework that leverages these expensive and inadequate expert demonstrations to teach a learner to perform a continuous control task efficiently. Trail transforms the expert's suboptimal demonstrations into a strict filter for the data used to train the learner's policy. By doing so, Trail ensures that any data used originates from a high-performing region of state and action spaces. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Trail by showing that it can produce a learner policy that meets certain criteria: it maintains a high level of performance when compared to the baseline policy that is trained without any constraints; it prioritizes high-reward states and actions over low-reward ones; and it reduces data requirements by a factor of nearly 30 for complex tasks.

Reinforcement learning-based training is commonly used for developing efficient and personalized automation systems. Yet, exploiting imitation learning can be beneficial as it allows the combination of human guidance with minimal requirements, leveraging expert input on critical tasks. A novel imitation learning technique known as co-imitation training is introduced, enabling the creation of automation systems that effectively learn from limited demonstrations shared among several human experts. By integrating their unique skills through a shared robot learning framework, the approach enables the development of a more capable and adaptable automation system that efficiently learns from a diverse range of human demonstrations. Experimental evaluations of co-imitation training demonstrate its potential to create automation systems that not only learn from multiple experts but also produce results comparable to those obtained through both expert-led reinforcement and combined imitation learning training. Furthermore, the intricacies of influencing automation behavior by rewriting the code are also explored.

This paper provides a geometric interpretation of a code's error correction capability, which can be calculated using the distance between a code's manifold and a sphere, especially for a class of codes known as partial alternating cycle codes. The paper also presents an efficient method for determining the minimum distance between a code's manifold and another given manifold. The minimum distance can also be determined for a class of code whose manifold has a specific underlying structure. The paper's findings can be applied to a type of code known as polar alternating cycle codes.

The replacement model approach has achieved significant success in neural machine translation, but a major limitation of current methods is the excessive computational expense associated with beam search. Our proposed solution is to treat beam search as an extensive action space problem and suggest several computationally efficient strategies for search that can be learned through reinforcement learning. We evaluate and compare eight variants of search strategies and demonstrate that several of these can achieve translation accuracy on par with the standard beam search at a substantially reduced computational cost. When integrating our methods into a sequence-to-sequence summation translation model, we find that the models we propose are not only more efficient but also produce more fluent translations of difficulty cases.

A collaborative system between a robot and a depth camera is utilized to achieve safe and precise cooperation. This research focuses on automating the collaboration without the need for external markers or alignment procedures. Initially, a mathematical model is developed to predict how the camera is positioned and adjusted relative to the robot. Next, an algorithm is implemented to calculate the camera's pose based on a 2.5D point cloud. The algorithm ensures that the collaboration is consistent with the conditions required for a stable and predictable joint effort. This is achieved through the execution of a program that checks the pose calculation before each collaboration. Consequently, this enables the automation of the collaboration without the need for human intervention. The results of the research are validated using a test environment and various test cases.

For a full strong Fock space $\mathcal{F}_\infty$, we define a subspace $\mathcal{L}^{(k)}$ in relation to the $k$th quasi-classical symplectic foliation. In essence, $\mathcal{L}^{(k)}$ encompasses elements in $\mathcal{F}_\infty$ characterized by polynomial assets in variables $x_j$ and their respective symplectic operators $\hat{x}_j$. We establish an integral representation for an arbitrary operator within $\mathcal{L}^{(k)}$, utilizing a generating function $B^{(k)}(x,\xi)$ that reflects the $k$th foliation and derives properties for operators within this space, including specific integral representations, and connections to Heisenberg algebras and Uhlmann's theorem. Moreover, we explore relationships between systems of algebras in $\mathcal{L}^{(k)}$ and their representations, establishing an explicit formula for the number of equivalent systems of algebras within a given space $\mathcal{L}^{(k)}$.

The consumption of online news is influenced by several factors including geographical location, political views, and online behavior. This study focuses on the impact of political beliefs on online news consumption patterns. A web scraping project was implemented to analyze over 1 million online comments made on news articles spanning 20 years, covering three presidential election cycles in the United States. The results revealed a significant shift in online news consumption habits based on political affiliation, with the divide increasing substantially leading up to the most recent election. Notably, research has shown that consumers with liberal viewpoints tend to engage more actively in online discussions than those with conservative views. Furthermore, Google search data analyzed over a decade highlights distinct patterns in search queries correlated with political affiliation, with some news outlets consistently aligning with the preferences of one affiliation over the other.

We examine the word problem for Thompson's group V by demonstrating that any two equivalent finitely generated subgroups have a common, finitely generated subset that includes words for 1 and the inverse of 1. This allows us to demonstrate that any two equivalent subgroups have a common, finitely generated subset that includes a subset that generates the whole group and has a specific countable set of elements. Additionally, this allows us to demonstrate that there exists a countable, finitely generated subgroup that is equivalent to the whole group.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly compelling due to the unique opportunities it provides for observing non-equilibrium steady states, which may exhibit richer properties than their equilibrium counterparts. In this work, we investigate the dynamics of a periodically driven single photon system, specifically focusing on the interplay between its absorption and emission processes as driven by a periodic source. Through both theoretical and experimental approaches, we found that, provided the drive is strong enough, the system reaches a steady state condition that is well described by a 2x2 matrix representation. The characterization of this steady state condition allows us to observe the non-trivial, entangled dynamics of the system's interaction with its surroundings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this condition can be modified by adjusting either the frequency of the drive or the rate at which the system's interaction with the surroundings changes.

We explore how various mechanisms including minimal curvature, concircular and conformal curvature exert their influence on an immersion of higher rank in the Euclidean space of dimension $n \geq 7$. Our findings reveal that if a hypersurface satisfies certain conditions including having a recurrent biharmonic adaptive curvature and meeting specific conformal and concircular requirements, its immersed form can be expressed as an isometric combination of a hypersurface with constant negative curvature and another with a conformally equivalent adaptive curvature. Furthermore, this conclusion can be extended to a hypersurface with a recurrent biharmonic $k$-adaptive curvature in the Euclidean space of dimension $n \geq 2k+3$.

A continuous distribution $Q$ among $p$ distinct points $x_1, \ldots, x_p$ relative to a ratio $q$ is considered $q$-identifiable if knowing the values of $Q(x_i)/Q(x_j)$ for all pairs $i$ and $j$ allows us to determine $Q$ up to a scalar factor. The term $q$-identifiable applies to any set $X$ that can be mapped one-to-one onto the set of the $p$ distinct points $x_1, \ldots, x_p$ by a monotonic function $f$. The purpose of this paper is to explore $q$-identifiable settings for continuous distributions on $X$ and to establish basic results about it. Specifically, it has been shown that any continuous distribution on $X$ can be determined up to a scalar factor if we have access to the values of the ratio of the distribution for all pairs of points in $X$. Moreover, it is demonstrated that if the monotonic mapping $f$ from $X$ to the $p$ distinct points $x_1, \ldots, x_p$ is twice differentiable, then the $q$-identifiable $X$ sets include those for which the derivative $f'$ never equals zero and does not change sign over $X$. The paper also investigates the issue of minimum entropy for identifiable distributions on various settings and identifies an identical formula for minimum

We investigate how new, shadowy matter components, which are formed by neutrinos interacting with a protracted axion field and possess non-standard properties, could influence cosmological phenomena. These shadow matter components, comprising three types of particles, are neutrinos with altered masses. As a result of this interaction, the primeval neutrino ensemble is divided into two distinct groups based on their cosmic behavior: a standard neutrino ensemble and a separate ensemble characterized by unusual properties. The unique characteristics of the latter ensemble are determined by the axion field's presence and, as such, are dependent on the ratio of the neutrino ensemble's initial density to its present form. If the shadow matter components' unique properties commence at a point in time when the Big Bang's primordial phases have already given way to a phase of rapid cosmological expansion, then the typical and unusual neutrino ensembles each behave in accordance with the cosmological principle. In this scenario, the unusual neutrino ensemble's density is proportional to the typical neutrino ensemble's density. If the unusual components' unique properties commence during the Big Bang's early phases, when the rapid expansion phase has yet to begin, then the typical and unusual neutrino ensembles each behave in accordance with the cosmological principle only up until a certain point in time, at which point their densities diverge. If the unusual components' unique properties commence before the onset of the rapid expansion phase, the unusual neutrino ensemble's density is proportional to the typical neutrino

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution fiber spectroscopic survey yielded around 620,000 spectra, with a typical exposure time of 1.5 hours. The medium-resolution fiber spectroscopic survey obtained around 220,000 spectra in 2-5 hours per exposure. The low-resolution survey detected around 13 million binary star candidates, as well as numerous candidate pulsars, cataclysmic variables, and other types of variable stars. The medium-resolution survey identified multiple binary star candidates, cataclysmic variables, and pulsars. This study highlights the scientific potential of time-domain observations using large optical photometric surveys and demonstrates how such surveys can be conducted with wide-field optical spectroscopic surveys using a type of telescope like the LAMOST.

In image recognition, using a fixed grid size can limit the detection of irregularly shaped objects. An alternative approach involves identifying and bounding such objects within a larger image volume. Researchers have proposed using fully convolutional networks (FCNs) for this task, but they often struggle to balance the extraction of feature information from medical images and the sequential bounding box data. To address this challenge, FCNs are often combined with FCN-based box proposal networks, leading to visually complex models. To circumvent this issue, we suggest integrating an FCN with a gate-controlled classifier, allowing the model to selectively focus on image features based on the current bounding box. By minimizing the attention mechanism, the proposed gate-controlled classifier provides a more direct and efficient way for the network to extract image data. By stacking this classifier, we can partition the image volume by semantic parts. Experimental evaluations on the LIDC dataset demonstrate that our proposed method achieves a mAP of 0.265 for irregularly shaped tumor detection, outperforming the baseline model by a significant margin.

MongoDB is a widely used NoSQL database that employs a transactional storage engine called the Distributed Transaction Coordinator (DTC). The DTC maintains data consistency across multiple shard nodes by managing transactions and updating version numbers. To ensure correctness, the DTC's storage module relies on a complex set of assumptions about the underlying data structure, which is referred to as transactional coherence. In our work, we investigate the behavior of the DTC's storage module and its impact on data coherence. We develop an automated verification approach using a finite-state machine model to formally prove that the DTC's storage module maintains transactional coherence. Our proof involves demonstrating that any execution of the storage module results in either a successful transaction or a conflict, which in turn confirms coherence. We have successfully applied our approach to verify version 3.6 and 4.0 of the DTC's storage module.

We establish the underlying positive structure of certain polynomial expressions known as chromatic symmetric functions, in the context of a specific combinatorial object called poset lattices. Our findings demonstrate that each element within this structure, specifically poset lattices consisting of a series of connected elements (poset lines), holds a distinct and non-decreasing combinatorial inductive property. Building upon this foundation, we prove the inductive property for poset lattices with any level of depth. Furthermore, we expand our results to poset lattices formed from multiple connected components. These outcomes enable us to display the underlying non-negative integer representation of each poset lattice, and subsequently, the coefficients of its characteristic polynomial and the inverse Kostka matrix.

We begin by defining a task where an agent must make informed decisions based on limited observations of a dynamic environment that changes over time. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of a dynamic state representation that captures essential information about the environment and refine it over time through a process of continuous revision. In our proposed approach, we incorporate a framework for reevaluating and recalibrating the representation by reconsidering previously held perceptions in light of subsequent experiences. This framework is underpinned by an explicit model of executive function that guides the process of revising the representation. When applied to the task of planning, our approach is equivalent to using a hindsight cost function to optimize future outcomes. Notably, our method shares a similar structure with the curriculum learning strategy, particularly in selecting the most relevant past experiences to build upon. Furthermore, our approach is a form of self-supervised learning where the agent actively seeks out new insights from its own internal perspective. When applied to the study of executive function, our method facilitates a deeper understanding of this cognitive process through a process of continuous reflection and refinement of the environment's representation.

The accuracy of medical image analysis models depends on their ability to overcome inherent biases present in pre-trained models and the datasets they are trained on. While various techniques have been developed to tackle bias, detecting the underlying causes remains a significant challenge. In this paper, the concept of intrinsic bias is introduced, referring to biases that are naturally occurring and cannot be removed by transforming the coordinate system. A statistical method was developed to quantify innate bias by comparing the distribution of characteristics in specific categories among medical image datasets. Experiments were conducted on three publicly available datasets for medical image classification, demonstrating that the proposed method effectively identifies innate bias by determining whether there is a significant disparity in the distribution of image attributes. The analysis revealed that certain datasets exhibit innate bias, confirming previous findings, while others did not exhibit this characteristic. Furthermore, the developed method was found to be more precise than existing comparison methods.

We introduce a novel strategy to distill the underlying geometry and dynamics of a complex system by using a topological transformation. This approach, which we call concealed dynamics, is illustrated through a study of Ising nanoassemblies that exhibit triangle-based coordination and are subject to both local and distant magnetic influences. By applying this technique to a highly coordinated system with long-range interactions, we gain a deeper understanding of how coordination, interaction strength, temperature, and spatial distribution combine to influence magnetic reversal patterns. Our findings reveal distinct patterns of coercivity versus coordination, and they are also reflected in temporal networks generated from time-series magnetization data. These patterns provide a clear indication of how a system's dynamics should be captured over time, and they demonstrate the critical role that temporal coordination plays in magnetic reversal processes.

The solar breeze, a flow of gas emanating from the Sun, gives rise to solar wind streams that interact with the innermost regions of our solar system. Due to the extreme conditions of the solar wind, previous observations were limited to measurements obtained from significant distances from the Sun. The close approach of the Parker Solar Probe allows for the study of solar wind behavior at much closer distances, and as a result, we can now directly observe the transition of solar wind streams into the undisturbed inner solar breeze. By examining energy flux measurements within the inner heliosphere, we find that in streams reaching the probe at distances of approximately 45 to 28 astronomical units from the Sun, energy flux exhibits a notable decrease, likely resulting from a reduction in Alfven wave power caused by the decreasing cross-sectional area of the stream as it approaches the critical point of formation. However, this decrease is not as pronounced at closer approach, and instead, we find energy flux to be significantly lower at 28 astronomical units, with a value of approximately 2.6 times that of Earth's magnetosphere, suggesting that the inner solar breeze may not have reached its critical point of formation even at this close approach.

Thanks to the widespread use and emotional interactions with social media and virtual assistants, understanding real people's emotions through speech has become a significant goal. Although significant progress has been achieved in modeling speech emotions using supervised deep learning methods with carefully curated datasets, there is still a major hurdle to overcome - adapting these models to work with untreated data from the real world. This paper proposes a innovative framework that employs transfer learning via deep reinforcement learning to adapt a pre-trained model on a large dataset to classify real-world emotions with just a limited amount of labeled data. Experimental results show that this framework yields a highly accurate model with a high mean average precision of 57%, significantly outperforming the baseline methods. This innovative approach has immense potential to enhance the emotional intelligence of virtual assistants and social media platforms by accurately detecting real-world emotions.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with rising pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.

Hybrid methods can solve discrete-continuous shortest path problems by dividing tasks into combinatorial and differentiable sub-problems. While effective, these methods rely on error-reducing techniques that converge to an optimal solution. However, the performance of these techniques is typically evaluated qualitatively or by examining individual instances. In our research, we develop a quantitative measure to analyze the error-reducing properties of these methods, which can be applied across various scenarios. To demonstrate the usefulness of this measure, we examine its effectiveness in reducing errors when solving a free flight trajectory optimization problem.

Researchers have previously discovered a unique cosmic structure - a spherical void within a uniformly expanding universe. In this study, we investigate the sudden appearance of a strong shock wave at the boundary of this spherical void. By applying conservation laws, we find that the shock's intensity is directly proportional to the square of the void's radius and is independent of the surrounding dense matter's specific properties. Conversely, the shock's temperature varies inversely with the square of the void's radius. These findings imply that large-scale structures like this void may provide valuable insights into understanding shock waves in the early universe.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadronic invariant mass. This rate is found to be 0.154 ± 0.015 nanoseconds when considering all $D_s^{*-}$ decays, and demonstrates a notable increase for certain final states, such as $D_s^{*-}\rightarrow K_{\rm S}^0\pi^{-}$.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advances made in classifying linear Schrödinger operators with rational potentials and fixed singularities, specifically focusing on those associated with the algebraic variety defined by the zero locus of a specific set of generalized Hermite polynomials. These advancements have resulted in a comprehensive listing of all possible combinations of spectral and symmetry characteristics for this class of Schrödinger operators. Building on earlier work by G. G. Emel'yanov, the current research establishes connections between the algebraic variety and another key concept, monodromy-free operators. It also establishes the equivalence of the latter being non-trivial and the absence of symmetry defined by the Z2 action, induced by the Schrödinger equation's time-reversal symmetry. Furthermore, the relationship between the algebraic variety and another important property, formed by combining two non-trivial symmetries, has been determined, leading to a subclassification of the former.

A persistent issue in signal processing research involves extracting meaningful information from rich time series data sets that are often marred by variability in both form and scale. As computational methods continue to excel at problem-solving, scientists are now applying them to investigate complex phenomena from physics to living systems, thereby uncovering common underlying principles. In this study, researchers combine advanced numerical techniques with careful data analysis to uncover hidden patterns in the time series behavior of an aging adhesive tape as it is slowly peeled apart. The tape's dynamic response reveals itself to be a self-similar fractal, with a distinct structure that is determined by just two parameters: the age of the tape and the force required to initiate peeling. This groundbreaking discovery paves the way for a deeper understanding of the intricate mechanisms driving temporal change, including those involved in the aging process itself. As a result, it is now possible to monitor the tape's internal state by analyzing any cross-sectional slice of the time series data, an advancement with far-reaching implications for scientific discovery and problem-solving.

The unique properties of superconducting matter are closely tied to the behavior of a superconducting phase, which is often measured using a Josephson junction's DC current-voltage characteristic in both magnetic field and temperature. To gain a comprehensive understanding of the phase, researchers have employed various methods to observe it, including transmission and reflection of superconducting quantum interferences, microwave power, and capacitance measurements. This paper compares and contrasts these different approaches to observing the phase, presenting a detailed temperature-magnetic field phase diagram for a typical grain boundary junction. The diagram shows distinct regions of nonlinear behavior, nonlinear capacitance, and microwave power transmission, which are derived from fundamental equations governing a Josephson junction. To further illustrate the relevance of these measurements, the paper also explores potential applications of nonlinear measurements in diagnosing and treating cardiac arrhythmias.

The Spinning-Particle-Irenee-Hui model incorporates a non-abelian ether-like term that affects the propagation of particles. In this research, the influence of finite temperature on the particle's spin, motion and temperature through a medium are extensively explored. Various thermal properties are derived from the modified equilibrium condition and detailed balance. These include temperature gradients that cause spin precession, diffusion coefficients and a thermal conductivity influenced by both the medium's properties and the particle's spin. Additionally, a distinction is made between the thermal conductivity of left- and right-circularly polarized particles.

This research formulates an analytical method for calculating the marginal cost of an option under a dynamic delta-hedging strategy, taking into account market impact and transaction costs. By assuming a specific relationship between the hedging strategy and market movements, a semi-analytical solution is derived for the expected cost of hedging, which can be applied to various probability distributions and even co-named options. The proposed method is efficient and can be implemented through a straightforward Monte Carlo simulation for specific parameters. However, it loses efficiency in those cases. The study finds that the most influential factor in determining hedging costs is the standard deviation of stock price movements, and the impact of transaction costs is proportional to this variable squared. The research also provides empirical evidence for its findings using real-world data and Monte Carlo simulations. The study's results demonstrate that the proposed equation can accurately predict hedging costs, outperforming alternative methods such as delta-gamma approximations. The study's findings are relevant to derivatives pricing, in particular the pricing of options under dynamic hedging, which is a well-established approach, and the study's methodology can be applied to other types of derivatives subject to hedging constraints.

This research focuses on the long-term behavior of a variety of mixtures with distinct properties, where the differential constraints represent the material's strength. Models incorporating high-contrast mixtures have historically been challenging to analyze due to their non-standard symmetry. This study utilizes the concept of relaxation to accommodate a wider range of material strengths, redefining the model as an optimal control problem. By reformatting the control problem as a system of partial differential equations with a mix of their highest and next-highest growth rates, the asymptotic behavior of the original model is determined through the application of H-convergence and the Asmussen-Leroux method. Specifically, the model's stationary solutions and the evolution equation's global behavior are both determined by the strongest component's properties.

We undertook a statistical investigation to determine the occurrence of tidal features around early-type galaxies that are massive. Our analysis was based on the wide-field imaging of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. We employed two methods to identify these tidal features: a curve fitting approach and a method using local flux fractions. The curve fitting approach yielded a rate of 12.9 percent, while the flux fraction method reported a rate of 8.4 percent. These rates varied in accordance with stellar mass, ranging from 5.6 percent for massive galaxies to a high of 14.5 percent among lower-mass galaxies. Additionally, we found that these features represented a significant fraction of the total galaxy mass, ranging from 1.3 to 4.5 percent, and that their shape resembled that of spiral galaxies in approximately 60 percent of cases. Our findings indicated that massive early-type galaxies are involved in major mergers at a rate of 0.4 per billion years, and that they are also subject to smaller, more disruptive interactions that go undetected.

A dynamic transmission model is proposed that incorporates opportunities as a fundamental component and enables the examination of intergenerational mobility over an infinite number of generations. The model is characterized by persistent differences in earnings and an exogenous rate at which children are born. In the absence of external influences, the model demonstrates that the distribution of earnings among newborn children is equal, and the same holds true for the distribution of opportunities among all existing individuals. However, when the rate of birth exceeds the rate of death, an uneven distribution of earnings and opportunities emerges, where those with more opportunities have a greater number of descendants. The model also reveals that the extent of this disparity is directly proportional to the difference between the rate of birth and the rate of death, and is therefore susceptible to change.

In the context of the energy sector, laser technology holds significant potential, with amplitude-shift-keying (ASK) being a widely adopted modulation technique. However, ASK's limited performance capabilities make 16-QAM (a more efficient modulation method) necessary for achieving high power levels. While 16-QAM can be efficiently converted back to ASK for use in power amplifiers, this process can introduce non-linear effects that compromise system performance. Given this challenge, this research focuses on designing a 2 GW-class, 1.75 $\mu$m wavelength 16-QAM system. To achieve this goal, existing laser systems were studied, with reverse engineering revealing the underlying structure and operating parameters, including temperature and voltage controls. Enhancements were then made to the temperature control mechanism to prevent thermal-induced distortions and ensure stable operation. Furthermore, numerical modeling validated the designed system's performance, showing minimal spectral and eye diagram changes when compared to the initial 1 GW-class prototype. Building upon previous work, this research demonstrates the feasibility of scaling high-power laser systems to multiple GW classes.

We demonstrate that for any given $1 < p \neq 2$ and any given $\delta > 0$, there exist quantifiable instances of $n$-dimensional $\ell_p$ spaces, denoted as $U$, such that for any isometric linear map $T$ from $\ell_p$, where the isomorphic dimension decrease ratio is greater than $\delta$, it follows that there exists an $\epsilon$-isometric linear subspace $W$ within $\ell_p$, with a dimension of at most $n$ and a $\ell_p$ unit ball that, under the application of $T$, results in a space that is greater than $\epsilon$-isometric from $W$. This theory builds upon previous research by D. K. Arora, L. Minkowski, and N. K. Shami for the case when $p=2$ and the case when $p \neq 2$.

As power levels increase on future particle accelerators, monitoring and maintaining beam quality become increasingly critical, necessitating the development of more sophisticated diagnostic tools. A promising method involves using scanning devices that sample the electromagnetic field emitted by a beam as it passes through a specific point, essentially taking a "photo" of the beam. By adjusting the configuration of the scanning device, this approach can provide detailed information about beam characteristics such as transverse size, distribution, and electromagnetic polarization. By collecting data across multiple directions, this method can even reveal information about the beam's longitudinal profile. This paper will explore the theoretical foundations and scanned signal processing techniques, in addition to presenting experimental results from the DAΦNE light beam scanner at the INFN Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in a distributed system consisting of multiple agents cooperating to minimize a collective objective function. The agents communicate with each other and a central coordinator through direct connections, while also exchanging information with neighboring agents in the network. The cooperation is compromised when one of the agents maliciously manipulates the shared information, forcing the other agents to recalculate their updates. To overcome this attack, we propose a new algorithm that combines a distributed optimization method with a gradient-based update strategy. The proposed algorithm treats the malicious attack as additional noise and optimizes a robust formulation by incorporating a penalty term into the objective function. We establish theoretsical convergence and stability analysis for the proposed algorithm and compare it to existing attack-free and strongest-attack-situation alternatives. Simulation results are also presented to illustrate the algorithm's effectiveness.

The analysis of cosmic microwave background experiments is subject to various instrumental limitations that affect their measurement of cosmological parameters. To accurately assess these measurements, it is essential to simulate the experiments' observational data realistically. While numerous tools simulate observations directly from first principles, they often lack the detail required to assess the impact of instrumental limitations on the measurements. In contrast, our processing pipeline takes into account the actual design specifications of experiments, such as beam shapes and sampling patterns, to simulate the biases inherent in their data. To verify the reliability of this approach, we compare the results of our pipeline with those of other simulation tools that simulate experiments' observations directly from first principles.

In this work, we investigate how pre-trained language models, specifically BART, achieve word order arrangements commonly seen in well-formed sentences. Through our analysis of 100 million training data, we identify that a substantial proportion of instances where BART fails to arrange words correctly are associated with poorly constructed questions, often mirroring the same order as the query. Interestingly, incorporating the original question as additional context significantly enhances BART's performance. Interestingly, incorporating the original question as additional context significantly enhances BART's performance. Furthermore, our findings suggest that leveraging contextual information beyond just the query can yield even greater improvements. To better comprehend BART's capacity for sentence generation, we also examine sentences comprising just two words. Interestingly, success in these tests is highly correlated with the statistics governing our analysis of longer sentences.

The proliferation of deepfake technology necessitates swift development of a countermeasure - a detection framework. Research in this area has yielded diverse approaches; nonetheless, a significant shortfall persists. To bridge this gap, our investigation introduces the MD-CSDNetwork model, a pioneering detection system grounded in a cross-stitching circuit possessing autonomous neural network loops. By incorporating a non-linear aggregation mechanism and cross-stitching connections, this system excels in combining feature extracts from input images and real/fake labels. Extensive experiments conducted on the CelebA, VGG-Face, and FaceForennsy datasets demonstrate the MD-CSDNetwork's superior performance compared to existing leading detection methods.

Current research on analyzing the performance of code constructions through studies of extreme properties in random graph ensembles has yielded significant progress. In this work, we extend this research by exploring new code constructions and performance assessments under a binary deletion channel by examining random graph ensembles with specific degree correlations in random graphs. We establish several performance metrics for the accuracy of these code constructions and derive general upper and lower bounds for the corresponding packet error probability in scenarios where the degree sequences follow a stationary ergodic process. We apply these general bounds to derive error probability upper and lower bounds for various code constructions, including regular low-density parity-check codes, code constructions with degree correlations that mimic the properties of a random regular graph, and a specific class of degree sequences with power-law characteristics. These analyses provide a clear understanding of the trade-offs between different degree sequences and their impact on the performance of code constructions under a binary deletion channel.

Previous research demonstrated the effectiveness of the decoy-state protocol in securely distributing quantum keys over an insecure environment. A random phase modulation of source laser, used to enhance the efficiency of this system, may however compromise its security. An analysis of the proposed phase modulation, incorporating a randomly generated phase for both the signal and decoy states, reveals its potential for system compromise. A novel approach to preventing this vulnerability involves introducing a non-random phase difference between the signal and decoy states.
