The underlying motivations of students, whether intrinsic or extrinsic, have been observed to significantly influence learning outcomes. Research into students' curiosity is valuable for developing strategies that foster curiosity in a way that learning outcomes are maximally amplified. Although previous studies have measured students' curiosity, they have primarily done so at a single point in time, neglecting the dynamic nature of curiosity. Moreover, conventional approaches have relied heavily on self-report surveys from individual perspectives, which may be limited by biases and lack the broader contextual learning dynamics. In contrast, our study proposes an integrated method that simultaneously monitors learning activities, classroom interactions, and emotional states to comprehensively capture the complex, temporal, and social aspects of curiosity. This novel approach enables the empirical analysis of curiosity's development over time within a specific learning context. We applied this approach to data from a physics lesson and used it to investigate how curiosity changes over the course of the lesson and varies across different students and learning states. Our findings suggest that curiosity exhibits distinct temporal patterns, and individual curiosity profiles are unique and linked to specific learning phases. Furthermore, we identified particular classroom interactions and emotional responses that are associated with curiosity's development. This study's integrated approach provides a framework for exploring curiosity's dynamics in a more nuanced and contextually rich manner, and its findings have implications for designing learning environments that foster curiosity's development.

This research introduces a novel parametric family of Gaussian random field models, centered on the Mat\'ern formula, that can be applied to any graph and a range of kernel functions. By characterizing the hyperparameter in terms of the graph's properties and establishing connections to random walk and graph Laplacian techniques, our approach extends and generalizes previous models such as the Gaussian Random Field and Lasso-Lama. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through multiple synthetic and real-world experiments, showing it achieves a better balance between model complexity and fit.

The growing number of ridesharing services has created a substantial amount of location data that can be utilized for detecting and monitoring urban road networks. Through the optimal placement of a limited number of vehicles within the network, we demonstrate that it is feasible to accurately detect all roads within the network. The scope of our research involves cooperation among vehicles, with each one responsible for a distinct segment of the network. We establish a model to gauge the effectiveness of our detection approach and the precision required for our method is shown to be directly proportional to the level of cooperation among vehicles, as expressed by the ratio of the number of vehicles to the number of network nodes. Furthermore, we verify the efficacy of our approach through simulations based on real-world data from New York City.

Researchers utilize effective field theories to analyze rare phenomena in high-energy environments, such as neutrino and dark matter, affecting observables in rare processes like $B$-decays and Higgs interactions. In this study, we examine the impact of the unknown photon plus missing energy in $J/\psi$ decays on these analyses. By comparing observed rates of $J/\psi\to \gamma\nu\nu$ to theoretical predictions, we determine the necessary neutrino mass matrix entries to be very small, thus not distorting $J/\psi$ decay patterns. As a result, we establish the constraints on parameters in various effective field theories, such as the neutrino subGeV dark matter sector, high-firmness lepton non-standard interactions, and a dark photon model with a small mass. These constraints already meet existing limits from colliders and other experiments.

Previous research introduced a new method called SDIMSIM for system differential equations, incorporating variable stepsize options. This study builds upon that work by fine-tuning the method for use on non-stiff problems, specifically obtaining an order of two when employing constant step sizes and successfully adapting the method to work with variable step sizes. Numerical experiments are also conducted to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

This work introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum examination (MFSSD) for analyzing multivariate functional time series data across various dimensional domains. Our research demonstrates that the MFSSD method yields reliable results when analyzing stochastic processes and is computationally efficient. Although it's an offline tool, we demonstrate that its components can be applied to real-time forecasting using nearby data. This research introduces key aspects of the methodology including parameter selection and multiple component interpretation. Our results show that the MFSSD method outperforms other methods in multiple scenarios. This work also offers a software package called RfSSA for users to access the methodology via a user-friendly interface.

Artificially engineered ecosystems of smartphones, known as smartphone sensing systems, have been utilized to monitor the behavior of individuals and intervene in their daily activities for both beneficial and malicious purposes. Although prior research has examined the effectiveness of these interventions, the underlying technology's stability and responsiveness in supporting successful outcomes remain unexplored. This paper investigates the responsiveness and stability of smartphone sensing systems through a theoretical framework that is validated by empirical data, ultimately revealing that existing systems are both prone to overreacting and overstating their effectiveness. To mitigate these issues, this paper presents defensive strategies that involve leveraging machine learning algorithms to prioritize interventions that promote long-term goal achievement and minimize the risk of system instability. When applied to a case study on reducing smartphone usage, the proposed methods yield results that highlight the challenges of achieving stable outcomes with existing systems and the potential benefits of defensive strategies in promoting more enduring goal achievement.

This study confirms the existence of a stationary phase for specific functions related to the local time of a random walk, essentially mapping onto the Airy function following time and space scaling parameters. Key insights emerge from comparing this result to the parabolic equation for the Airy operator, which has a well-documented stationary phase property. In contrast, the Gaussian rescaled parabola does not support a persistent phase in either the walk's positive or negative directions. Some general implications for the random walk's local time and its associated capacity are also derived.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves used for heating and current drive in tokamaks. Operating at 13.5 MHz, the facility features a helicon-type plasma source that produces plasma through a radio frequency coil and serves as a key component in the investigation. Due to the source's significant influence on measurement results, it was essential to thoroughly assess its performance. Studies revealed that the plasma produced met essential requirements for mimicking edge plasmas found in tokamaks, with key characteristics including temperature ranges (1.3-2.5 eV), electron densities (0.8-3 x 10^19 m^-3, controlled by the source's power), and a negative potential (around 2V) that accords with observations from tokamaks using spectrometry techniques. Notably, the research demonstrated that high-density plasmas (above 1.5 x 10^19 m^-3) exhibited features consistent with the formation of a sheath plasma, driven by electron emission from the end plates, which may have implications for edge plasmas in tokamaks.

In contrast to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit distinct characteristics where the pathogens used exhibit similar needs to the target pests and have a reduced impact on other beneficial pests. This paper explores a simplified model featuring predator-prey relationships, where the pathogens utilized in microbial pesticides are used in conjunction with chemical pesticides. By drawing from classical Lyapunov theory and the Laslettie-Wazner theorem, this paper investigates the local stability of the model's equilibrium point and phase plane analysis is conducted to examine boundary dynamics.

This study presents a novel approach, W-Net, for automatically identifying and
delimiting cell nuclei in histopathological images. The team demonstrated the
efficacy of this method by conducting experiments using three diverse datasets
and reported encouraging results. Notably, W-Net excelled in accuracy when
comparing it to existing literature. To further validate the performance, the
study employed two additional evaluation metrics and demonstrated robust
results. Furthermore, the investigation included an in-depth analysis of
experiments with varying hyperparameters and a comprehensive evaluation of
feature importance.

Let's consider an algebraically closed field $K$ of characteristic not equal to $2$. We will examine local non-standard forms on specific classical groups - specifically the odd special orthogonal group $SO_n(K)$ for $n \geq 5$ and the symplectic group $Sp_n(K)$ for $n \geq 3$. Our analysis focuses on whether these forms are standard or isotopic to a standard form when they have a specific maximal associative polynomial invariant. This question has been answered in previous works for standard forms and for non-standard forms in characteristic zero. Our main contribution is to extend this result to fields of positive characteristic.

A graph G is considered traceable if a Hamiltonian path exists between any pair of vertices. Repeated line graphs of a graph G, denoted as L^k(G), are constructed by applying the line graph operation k times to G. This paper focuses on examining the properties of repeated line graphs in relation to their hamiltonian path index (HPI), specifically by exploring what values of k would ensure that L^k(G) is a traceable graph. Some current limitations and related conjectures on this topic are also discussed.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute significantly to the high mortality rates associated with SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia. Pyroptosis development is driven by the NLRP3 inflammasome's activation of caspase-1, which in turn cleaves IL-1β into its active form. This study aims to create a single-cell mathematical model that captures the biological processes leading to pyroptotic cell death and explores how anti-inflammatory interventions impact this pathway. The model specifically examines the NLRP3 inflammasome's assembly, caspase-1 activation, and IL-1β maturation, as well as the cell's response to various treatments such as glucocorticoids, which can repress the NLRP3 inflammasome and caspase-1 activity. By simulating these processes, we have derived a model that describes how treatment affects the probability of pyroptotic cell death and is supported by existing research. This model can be applied to investigate the efficacy of different treatment schedules in preventing pyroptotic cell death and has implications for our understanding of the NLRP3 inflammasome's dynamics within a single cell.

External influences affecting states and reward signals can mislead reinforcement learning agents, hindering their ability to achieve optimal performance by introducing irrelevant information about the environment's internal dynamics. In this research, we develop a theoretical framework to identify and remove states and rewards that are entirely extrinsic to the system being controlled, leading to a streamlined set of variables that the agent can use to maximize its efficiency. Our analysis leverages a library of pre-existing modular components and proves the existence of an optimal agent configuration by applying a fundamental theorem. To illustrate our approach, an example model demonstrates how an external reward can be derived from an uninformative state variable. Further, we explore the implications of our framework for developing innovative reinforcement learning agents and examine the connection to established paradigms.

A blockchain-based smart contract is considered reliable if it accurately meets the expectations of its users across various networks. However, the lack of standardization in error reporting across different blockchain platforms makes validation challenging. To overcome this obstacle, our project HELMHOLTZ is developed as a refinement-type contract validator for the Tezos blockchain, allowing users to verify the correctness of their contracts through a static analysis method. By leveraging refinement types from the Idris programming language, contractors can express and validate the behavioral properties of their code. A key feature of HELMHOLTZ is its ability to generate detailed error messages similar to those produced by the Smart-Check validator, enabling users to thoroughly assess the correctness of their contracts.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained remarkable popularity in processing complex and irregular data structures such as images and videos, and are well-suited for analyzing interconnected node relationships found in graphs. Although GCNNs outperform traditional methods in many applications, the lack of a clear and intuitive understanding of their workings hinders further development and refinement. In an effort to address this knowledge gap, we delve into the inner workings and derivative-based optimization process of GCNNs, matching each layer's operation to a corresponding filter that aligns with the network's overall learning objective. This unified view provides a foundational basis for exploring and refining the extensive array of GCNN variants available.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is modified to include a scalar field with a non-zero mass, resulting in the formation of solitons and rotating black holes with a scalar "hair." This modification leads to solitons with non-zero electric and magnetic charges, as well as rotating black holes that exhibit the same charge properties. These solitons and black holes can be represented by an artificial Chern-Simons term. The Chern-Simons action gives rise to a conserved quantity, linked to the solitons' and black holes' charge and angular momentum characteristics. The relationship between the Chern-Simons term and the conserved quantity is established through the Einstein scalar field's dynamics. The conserved quantity can be expressed as a sum of the electric and magnetic charges and the angular momentum divided by two. The charge properties of the solitons and black holes can also be described using the Chern-Simons term's geometric interpretation. The Chern-Simons term's surface integral across the event horizon of a rotating black hole with a non-zero electric charge indicates that the scalar "hair" is linked to the angular momentum and the presence of an "electric mirror" soliton. The presence of a magnetic charge in these black holes and solitons represents an "embedded" soliton with the opposite magnetic charge. The relationship between the Chern-Simons term and the conserved quantity is used to identify new "mirror" solitons with a non-zero electric

We've observed a novel phenomenon in systems with reversible symmetries, where the thermal equilibrium configurations are isotropic and display Bragg-like blurring. This peculiar behavior is unique to systems with reversible symotries, and we've found that any irreversible symmetry disrupts this phenomenon, leading to anisotropic thermal equilibria that exhibit crystal-like patterns. This discovery implies that certain non-reversible transformations can induce a shift from bragg-like blurring to crystal-like patterns, and we've demonstrated this by applying a specific non-reversible transformation to a system with reversible symmetries - the motion of a brane within that system.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualization of tissue pathologies by highlighting the mechanical characteristics of tissues. However, accurate estimation of mechanical properties is hampered by significant uncertainties originating from insufficient spatial resolution in recorded ultrasound data and estimation algorithms. The conventional approach to elastography involves generating an estimate of Young's modulus through comparison of pre- and post-stimulation ultrasound data sets. However, this method fails to consider the virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique's high spatial resolution and precise estimation capabilities. We propose integrating the VSSA method with elastography to enhance the estimation of mechanical properties. Specifically, we utilize the VSSA technique for receiving ultrasound data after tissue stimulation and derive a new formula for estimating the speed of the shear wave. Numerical simulations and in vitro experiments validate the proposed approach, yielding a 6.5 times improvement in estimation accuracy compared to the conventional method.

We introduce a new, flexible approach to writing pseudocode, which incorporates variables representing unknown inputs and output variables for the algorithm's results. This approach, called Logical Pseudocode, makes use of first-order logic variables and includes comments that are statements in a form of predicate calculus. We demonstrate the feasibility of our method by creating examples of Logical Pseudcodes for several classic problems, including finding prime factors, solving linear congruences, and discovering minimum circumscribed boxes.

The concept of Ramsey minimality character a poset $P$ with respect to another poset $Q$, which was introduced by Neumann-Lattorff and Haviar, can be interpreted through the lens of combinatorial game theory. This paper delves into a specific category of posets known as $V$-shaped posets and explores their Ramsey characteristics within the Boolean lattices of four elements when the Schauder height between the source and target posets exceeds one. Building on earlier research by Haddad and Jost, we establish upper bounds for the Ramsey number $r^{2^{4}-1}(K_{n},K_{m})$ for all V-shaped intervals with $n, m \geq 3$, and derive lower bounds for some instances, including those with $n,m \geq 4$. Notably, we find the Ramsey number $r^{2^{4}-1}(K_{3},K_{3})$ which had gone unresolved in previous studies. This work also extends the available methods to determine upper bounds for a broader range of V-shaped posets.

In the context of a dynamic $k$-centers clustering, where the clustering model and the parameter $k$ remain unknown, a series of points arrive one by one, and each point has a limited observation of the previous points, including the current center of the clustering model. The goal is to determine the number of centers, remove the model's ambiguity, and recover the clusters by selecting a subset of previously identified centers as the final $k$-centers. Based on a new metric that captures the ambiguity of the clustering model, we establish a lower bound of approximately $d^2 \cdot (k-1)^2 \cdot 4^k$ information-theoretic interactions to solve this problem in general scenarios. For high-dimensional data in the presence of a large $k$, we prove a nearly optimal dynamic $k$-centers clustering solution, and our approach demonstrates significant improvement over standard multi-armed bandit methods. Additionally, we validate our theoretical findings with extensive numerical experiments.

We introduce a novel class of stochastic chase-evasion games, a complex category that encompasses various scenarios including those played on high-dimensional state spaces in the context of autonomous vehicles. Building upon the theory of dynamic programs with functional decision rules, we establish a general framework for efficiently solving these games by dividing them into a hierarchy of smaller, more manageable components. Key aspects of our approach include the creation of an optimal localized policy for a 'core' component, which is then used to inform the development of effective hierarchical policies. Through the application of our methodology to a a series of chase-evasion scenarios, we demonstrate a substantial reduction in computation required, exceeding even current state-of-the-art parallelization methods.

Bayesian inference employs the concept of likelihood to update the probability of a specific hypothesis by considering the evidence provided by a particular observation. However, issues arise when the likelihood function is nontransitive, meaning that the comparison of the likelihood of one event to another depends on a third event. This problem is often addressed by requiring the likelihood function to be cyclic in the sense that if the likelihood of A over B is greater than the likelihood of B over C, then the likelihood of C over A must be greater than the likelihood of A over B. We contend that this property is more relevant than transitivity and demonstrate several nontransitive likelihoods that satisfy cyclic transitivity. We also examine the relationship between the likelihood and the posterior distribution and demonstrate the implications of cyclic transitivity in the context of a model selection paradigm.

Recently, deep learning-based techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, but applying these methods on a large scale is costly and impractical due to the necessity of obtaining a large dataset of paired high-dose and low-dose images. An alternative approach is restoring low-dose CT images through an unsupervised transformation using CycleGAN, a model that requires no pairings and can convert high-dose images into high-dose images, but has limited success in image enhancement. In this paper, we modify the CycleGAN architecture by introducing an AdaIN layer in the synthesis pathway, allowing us to switch the layer's operation from a non-linear generation to a linear transformation that mimics the identity transformation. This modification enables us to reuse the generator network for both training and testing phases. We also introduce two new loss functions to guide the unsupervised restoration process. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art models in preserving structural details, enhancing image quality, and reducing noise.

Current dialog understanding evaluations rely heavily on fully featured goal-oriented datasets with the task, support, and target labels all included. Nonetheless, such datasets are scarce and often don't accurately reflect real-world situations due to their limited scope and focus solely on straightforward fact-feeding conversations. Real-world dialog typically involves more complex interactions with various formats, like e-commerce websites and customer support platforms. As a result, future research should prioritize the semi-supervised pre-training of dialog models to improve their overall performance. To address this need, we introduce SPACE-2, a high-performance model that leverages contrastive learning for semi-supervised pre-training on dialog datasets, with special features like hierarchical structures and mask tactics. Extensive experiments showed that pre-trained SPACE-2 significantly outperforms baseline models and even achieves impressive results when compared to other strong competitors, with a notable 6.8% improvement on the DSTC9 final test leaderboard. Moreover, SPACE-2 exhibits remarkable generalization by demonstrating a 10% boost in performance when tested on a different goal-oriented dataset following the same target.

This research aims to explore the geometric characteristics of an ideal fluid spacetime that is equipped with a conformal Ricci-Yamabe metric and an equation derived from the conformal Ricci-Yamabe soliton. We have successfully demonstrated that when the conformal vector field generates a soliton in this ideal fluid spacetime, it results in a stable soliton. Additionally, we have established that the ideal fluid spacetime's potential $\phi$ is constant, and we have obtained a precise expression for this constant. Furthermore, we have derived a practical formula to determine whether the soliton is contractive, expansive, or rigid based on the ideal fluid spacetime's potential and the soliton's contraction or expansion coefficient.

To study the rotational characteristics of exotic nuclei, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Specifically, our research focused on three halo nuclei - $^{42}$Mg, $^{44}$S, and $^{44}$K - and their rotational excitations in 1d ($x$-direction) symmetry axes. We discovered that distortions in these nuclei lead to non-spherical shapes and cause rotational excitations to couple from the ground state, resulting in complex patterns of energy increase with spin. This phenomenon provides a clear understanding of how exotic properties in nuclei can be described through relativistic mean-field theory and the importance of considering shape decoupling effects in rotational excitations.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by integrating guided propagation and a deformable alignment technique to more effectively exploit temporal information, primarily employing the hourglass transformer for feature extraction and aggregation. We also introduce a simple yet effective way to enhance training efficiency and generalize the method to video interpolation. Our experiments demonstrate that the upgraded model achieves superior performance and versatility across SR and interpolation tasks.

The vector boson approximation, widely employed in high-energy collisions at muon colliders due to its computational efficiency and accurate representation of $W$ and $Z$ boson interactions, is scrutinized in this study. Our calculations yield a level of precision that exceeds 90% for the ratio of observable quantities beyond a confidence threshold of 95%. This level of precision is maintained even in scenarios where energy levels approach the mass of these vector bosons. Furthermore, our research indicates that the vector boson approximation can be relied upon in muon colliders, providing a computationally feasible solution for a potentially insurmountable computational bottleneck in peak luminosity requirements.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit from the overlap between tasks by minimizing catastrophic interference
and adapting existing task knowledge. While this concept is well-established in
supervised and online reinforcement learning settings, few studies have explored
its implications in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. We examine
this phenomenon by testing a fundamental question: Do learned models benefit
from being free from catastrophic interference, and do they generalize better to
new tasks when they are? To answer this, we developed a suite of complex,
continuous multi-task tasks that can be solved through planning and conducted
a series of experiments to evaluate how models and policies are affected by
being shared and learned for each individual task independently. Our results
show that model-based multi-task reinforcement learning can be more effective
when it avoids catastrophic interference and that it is crucial to select tasks
that are closely related and have significant overlap in their solution structures
to maximize this benefit. Additionally, we discovered that learning separate
models can lead to a more robust performance when compared to a single combined
model. Our work lays the groundwork for a more in-depth study of how to select
tasks in a multi-task reinforcement learning setting.

The paper provides derivations of Li-Yau, Souplet-Zhang, and Chen-Yang type estimates for the equation $u_t=\Delta_\xi p + \lambda u + A(u)$ in a complete, non-compact metric measure space with a compact boundary. Furthermore, the paper also establishes the comparison of the obtained estimates with previous results.

Kurt Godel, along with colleagues Alonzo Church, Stephen Kleene, and Rosser, first discussed the concept of a universal theorem in 1930. Not long after, Godel, in his famous 1930 lecture, referred to the potential for a universal theorem to be used in a diagonalization argument. In 1931, Godel published his famous incompleteness theorems, and the following year Church proved the existence of a universal theorem. In the early 1930s, Kleene and Rosser developed methods for constructing models that avoided the possibility of a universal true sentence existing, achieving this by essentially 'killing' any universal sentence through their construction. This work predates the development of computability theory and Kripke's schema, and demonstrates that a significant portion of the intuitive basis for the incompleteness theorems can be derived solely from the properties of computability.

This paper formalizes the three-ball conjecture for a specific partial differential equation - the Dirac equation - within the framework of complex variable theory. By treating functions of three real variables as functions of a special type of complex variable, we establish and prove a relevant average value theorem. The approach utilized in this paper is based on an equivalent representation of the Dirac equation in a special type of complex variable framework, known as monogenic functions. Building on earlier work by M. A. Mughal and R. K. Singh, we expand on their result by introducing specific modifications, including altering the radius of the inscribed sphere to 'r/4' and exploring average value theorems for higher order derivatives. The provided proof leverages techniques from monogenic function theory, particularly involving the Laplace operator and the Cauchy-Reimann equations.

The problem of selecting sampling locations is critical in numerous applications, significantly influencing the results of subsequent sampling and data collection methods such as quadrature, field measurements, and remote sensing. When dealing with geospatial data, neighboring points often have correlated values, which can lead to suboptimal performance when using traditional methods that disregard spatial structure. In this paper, a new approach is presented that leverages statistical models to model data correlations and vary the spacing of samples based on estimated gradients, equidistically placing samples in areas of varying density. We evaluate and compare our method to established approaches through the use of synthetic and real-world datasets, showing it yields improved performance.

In robotics, adjusting an end-mounted camera to match the orientation of an object is a challenging problem that has not yet been fully resolved. Current methods can often locate object features but struggle to accurately determine the camera's optimal orientation. A novel approach has been proposed that leverages machine learning to tackle this issue using only one image per object. The method first identifies key features, establishes point-to-point correspondences, and then employs a deep learning network to refine the camera's orientation. Comprehensive tests conducted with a variety of objects demonstrate that this method can effectively find the optimal camera orientation with a high degree of accuracy.

We tackle the challenge of solving inverse problems by generating a realistic image of the original object from an image of the distorted object. Our main difficulty lies in constructing a well-defined and consistent formulation for the problem, as the original object's possible images are derived from probability distributions associated with data that is inherently noisy. To address this issue, we develop a regularized conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that takes into account the inherent noise within the data. The proposed method allows us to derive a consistent and well-defined formulation for solving the inverse problem, and is flexible enough to be applied to various types of data and regularity constraints. Through numerical experiments and comparisons with other reconstruction methods, we demonstrate the superior performance of our method.

This article examines the concept of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a review of existing approaches used to identify surfaces that remain unaltered over time and discuss recent methods for determining the long-term behavior of systems. A specific technique is employed to eliminate surfaces that remain unchanged, and this is applied to a significant class of systems. Additionally, new results are obtained that provide nonexistence proofs for surfaces that remain unaltered in time.

Due to the limited coverage of THz communication's line-of-sight range, beam training is crucial for establishing high-quality connections in this frequency band. However, the time-consuming nature of traditional beam training techniques can conflict with the transient nature of indoor applications, where users are constantly moving and creating new channel conditions. In response, we propose an adaptive, learning-based approach that efficiently updates beam information over time. By leveraging reinforcement learning to update and refine the optimal beam in response to changing channel conditions, this approach can significantly reduce the time required for beam formation and improve the overall performance of the system. In our analysis, we develop a mathematical model of the proposed system and simulate various scenarios to demonstrate the advantages of our method. Notably, our results show that the new approach can achieve data transfer rates up to 10 times faster and reduce errors by 90% under certain conditions.

The interstellar medium is home to numerous structures that affect radio wave propagation. Researchers are working to map these structures by analyzing the effects of scintillation on radio signals from pulsars. This paper focuses on the relationship between scintillation patterns and structures in the line of sight to the pulsar B1133+16. By analyzing this relationship, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the scintillation patterns and the underlying structures. The duration and variability of scintillations in B1133+16's signal provide a measure of the density variations in the line of sight. However, the limited data available for this study restricts the scope of analysis to structural scales exceeding 30 AU. The results indicate that the scintillation components in B1133+16's signal remain stable over a period of several weeks to several months, with some variations observed in their amplitude. The study also reveals the presence of additional structure in the direction towards the pulsar, distinct from the main structure associated with the Local Bubble, particularly in the frequency 4.0 GHz and Earth velocity frame of reference. The study suggests conducting further research on the relationship between scintillation patterns and structures in the line of sight to the pulsar, including a more in-depth analysis of the data at frequencies 3.0 GHz and 6.0 GHz, as well as the effects of the Earth's motion on scintillation components.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the original WaveNet model. WaveNet's success in modeling various applications is attributed to its ability to learn feature representations and generate realistic outputs. However, this model struggles with capturing long-distance dependencies and fails to incorporate pitch information into its expanded convolutional layers. To address these limitations, our model includes a hierarchical structure that leverages pitch information to expand the network's layers, enabling the generation of high-quality audio samples. Experimental results show that QPNet outperforms the original WaveNet model and a pitch-independent variant in terms of mean opinion score (MOS) evaluations.

We introduce MADARi, an innovative annotation and correction platform for Arabic morphological analysis. Building on existing research, MADARi incorporates a range of features to streamline and refine the process of annotating and standardizing Arabic text morphologies. By providing a user-friendly interface and a robust backend system, MADARi enables a substantial increase in efficiency and productivity in both rule-based and machine learning approaches to Arabic NLP tasks. Additionally, the platform facilitates the development of large-scale annotated corpora for these tasks.

Planets similar to Earth, orbiting stars like the Sun, have a high potential for supporting life. However, the conditions on these planets can be vastly different from those on Earth due to various factors including their atmospheric composition, temperature, and the intensity of their starlight. To effectively study these planets, NASA's Terrestrial Planet Finder and James Webb Space Telescope are being designed to observe and analyze the light that these planets reflect. By understanding how these exoplanets interact with their starlight, we can gather valuable information about their atmospheres and surfaces. Using numerical simulations, we simulated the light that hundreds of exoplanetes reflect, taking into account their varying shapes, sizes, and temperatures as well as different atmospheric compositions. We extracted specific spectral characteristics from this light to help guide the scientific instruments being developed for the JWST and TPF. By taking these considerations into account, we believe we can increase our ability to identify and analyze the conditions on these planets by 10 times over current methods.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves modifying the tunneling spectroscopy setup to incorporate a high resistance material in the electrode, effectively increasing the Ohmic dissipation to the point where it surpasses the peak height. This modification has both theoretical and practical advantages. The theoretical benefit lies in the fact that even tiny non-zero temperatures can distinguish between the two phenomena, leveraging the disparity in behavior between Majorana and non-Majorana peaks under conditions of tunneling when there's significant Ohmic dissipation. The practical advantage stems from the use of a simple and easily adjustable setup that only requires tweaking the electrode's resistance level to achieve the desired outcome. The proposed approach is equally applicable to various proposed methods for detecting Majorana fermions.

The development of advanced materials in road construction has accelerated, allowing roads to last longer. As a result, the frequency of road repairs has increased, making it essential to develop efficient automated systems for detecting and maintaining roads. This detection and maintenance process involves several challenges, including the need to collect and manage substantial data, gather information from multiple sources, and Pronto's limited availability for road inspection. To address these issues, we present RoadAtlas, a pioneering system that utilizes AI and multi-sensor technology to identify defects on roads during regular vehicle operations. RoadAtlas enables real-time data processing and automated flaw detection using machine learning algorithms. It also offers a user-friendly interface for data analysis and is compatible with various programming languages for custom extensions. Through data sharing and coordinated efforts, RoadAtlas can reduce road inspection costs and minimize downtime between regular inspections. By integrating with existing infrastructure, it can detect and address potential flaws more effectively.

We establish a direct connection between shadows, a well-known class of subspaces in convex geometry, and bicategories by drawing parallels to the relationships between categories, simplicial spaces, and geometric realizations. This connection allows us to define subobjects within a bicategorical context that correspond directly to shadows. Building on this connection, we explore additional properties of subobjects in a bicategorical setting, including the association with bimodal spaces and the extension to colored versions.

We introduce a challenging new task called visual noise localization, where the objective is to identify the specific location within an image where a randomly occurring pixel anomaly is present. This task is distinctive because it's impossible to determine the answer without first examining the entire image. We establish a robust method for evaluating models that attempt to tackle this problem and propose several models of varying complexity to test their performance. Our research indicates that models excel at predicting the overall image section that contains the anomaly but struggle to accurately pinpoint the exact location within that section. We introduce the concept of model intractability and its relationship to the way information is organized within an image, and explore different patterns models use to make predictions. Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for the broader field of image classification.

Multi-layer graph neural networks are typically characterized by their ability to effectively
embed graph structures within a hierarchical framework, achieving impressive performance
in various benchmarking tasks such as node classification, link prediction and graph
classification. However, a major limitation of most graph neural networks is their
geometric coherence, with many models exhibiting anomalous distances between node
embeddings, particularly as the network depth increases. To address this issue, we
propose a novel non-Euclidean graph neural network model based on the Lorentzian
manifold, which incorporates a novel hyperbolic contrastive loss function to
enforce geometric coherence within node embeddings. Our model achieves superior
performance compared to its Euclidean-based counterparts across 5 distinct GNN
tasks, in addition to reducing overfitting and accelerating training speed.

The primary objective of an inverse problem is to determine the underlying structure or key properties of a system by making observations of a system's behavioral output. In contrast, the 'inverse challenge' refers to a scenario where the primary goal is to intentionally alter a system's behavior based on its internal structure or key properties. This work focuses on an acoustic structure interaction problem, where the task is to intentionally create a specific sound pattern within a given enclosure by manipulating the boundary conditions on an adjacent plate. A non-destructive approach, utilizing measurement of the plate's vibration as an observing system, is employed to achieve this outcome. This methodology leverages an operator theoretical framework, specifically the use of a single layer operator and its inverse, to reconstruct the boundary condition on the plate. A numerical implementation of this process has been carried out and the resulting code has been utilized to conduct several simulations.

The intersection of mechanical and optical systems, known as optomechanics, has introduced novel methods for studying quantum dynamics within coupled systems. A particular area of interest involves a three-part configuration consisting of an optical cavity connected to a beam splitter, which in turn is linked to a mechanical oscillator. Our research delves into the quantum preservation of a single photon when an intense coherent light is used to drive the cavity, with the possibility of transferring it to the mechanical oscillator over time. A key finding shows that the rate at which this transfer occurs can be controlled through the interaction strengths of the optomechanical and beam-splitters, allowing it to be synchronized with the expected outcome. In particular, Steady-state compression transfer phenomenon emerges where the probability of transferring a photon from the optical cavity to the mechanical oscillator is maximized, however this requires the interaction between the optical cavity and beam splitter to be stronger than with the mechanical oscillator.

We integrate the modal $\mu$-calculus with a fragment of first-order logic over structured objects, expanding the modal $\mu$-calculus to express properties of entities within these structures. The extended calculus maintains the same depth of nested fixpoints as the original modal $\mu$-calculus while surpassing its expressive power. By applying nested games with alternating least and greatest fixpoints between premisses and conclusions, we prove the validity of the theorem: every formula in the enriched calculus can be proven valid through a sequence of formulae each of which is in one-to-one correspondence with the original modal $\mu$-calculus theorem. Furthermore, we establish that the complexity of the theorem-proving method matches the complexity of the modal $\mu$-calculus theorem-proving method.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating the variability in delay preferences, which is in line with recent research indicating that individuals' preferences for delayed rewards exhibit instability and are influenced by the length of delay. This new model effectively integrates the concepts of time-dependent preferences and time-dependent sensitivity to consequences through the use of the Tsallis exponent. We contend that individual parameters within this model reflect time-dependent sensitivity to consequences and time-dependent delay preferences, respectively. Furthermore, we suggest that the Tsallis exponent parameter governs delay discounting variability, with lower values indicating greater variability in delay preferences. We support our model with empirical data from a previously analyzed sample of 500 participants, finding that the Tsallis exponent parameter is a key driver of delay discounting variability. If our model is to be of use in policy-making or clinical applications, we believe it would require careful validation through further empirical research.

When formulating Hefty gravity within the context of metric-compatible gauge theories for second-order symmetric covariation fields, a specific harmonic gauge that yields a consistent and well-defined variational principle has been identified. This note examines an alternative gauge that emerges from a specific redefinition of the covariation fields' potentials, resulting in a formulation equivalent to Hefty gravity.

A signed graph is created by adding a polarity to the edges of an existing undirected graph. By extending the concept of an odd subgraph from G, which refers to any subgraph of G that contains an odd number of vertices and has a specific connection configuration, we can determine that the number of homomorphisms from an odd subgraph of a specific size to a signed graph G is directly related to the size of G when G has a particular property, or is bounded by a specific value when G does not have that property. However, if we remove the requirement for a specific connection configuration from the definition of an odd subgraph, the number of homomorphisms from such a subgraph to a signed graph G is not always directly related to the size of G or bounded by a specific value, as it also depends on the particular configuration of the subgraph. By introducing the concept of a strongly connected double cover of a connected graph G, which consists of two disjoint copies R and S of G and a set of matching edges between them, we can determine that the number of homomorphisms from a strongly connected double cover of a specific size to a signed graph G is directly related to the size of G when G has a particular property, or is bounded by a specific value when G does not have that property, as it also includes certain configurations of double covers that are not necessarily strongly connected.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium states, using the Weyl-Wigner representation, to be centered at specific points on the phase space, with their spreads determined by the parameters of a given system. This observation provides a geometric interpretation of the quantum thermodynamic phenomenon known as the equipartition theorem. A related transformation of symbols highlights the motion of thermal equilibrium states as the system's energy changes.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both specific microscopic models and the broader thermodynamic temperature framework. We examine the commonalities and distinguishing features of different approaches to defining negative temperature, including an investigation of the requirements for a system's energy spectrum that must be met to consider its temperature as genuinely negative. We also discuss the distinction between the Zeeman shift in atomic physics, which can result in negative temperature readings, and the broader thermodynamic context. Finally, we outline the prerequisites for achieving negative temperature states of matter, which involve both non-degenerate energy spectra and the ability to selectively populate higher-energy levels.

Let G be an abelian group and A a nonempty subset of G, with the restricted signed sumset denoted as kA,d consisting of elements that can be expressed as the linear combination of elements from A, with coefficients ranging from -d to d, and the requirement that the sum of the coefficients equals k. In this paper, we establish a minimum bound for the size of kA,d when A has a certain cardinality, and further investigate the problem of determining whether given cardinalities can yield a sumset of a specific size. Additionally, we derive lower and upper bounds for the size of kA,d when A consists of multiple disjoint subsets. These findings extend and generalize previous research on the subject.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to determine whether they have the potential to become malignant. This process involves examining tissue samples from the colon and rectum under a microscope to identify specific abnormalities. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved image classification accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated images. In this context, we've developed the UniToPatho dataset, comprising histopathological images of colorectal polyps along with grade labels from low to high severity. This dataset distinguishes UniToPatho from other collections by incorporating a broader range of abnormalities and incorporating expert opinions from multiple pathologists. It also surpasses existing datasets in terms of size. We've leveraged the UniToPatho dataset to train and test a deep learning model, achieving a notable 83.1% accuracy rate in classification and a Mean Absolute Error of 1.17 in grading. This work demonstrates the potential for deep learning to support the grading and classification of colorectal polyps, ultimately contributing to early detection and treatment of malignant lesions.

A novel numerical strategy is presented for solving a wide range of high-frequency time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around objects with smoothly varying material properties that refract rather than reflect waves. This approach leverages an innovative boundary layer approximation that adapts mesh size based on local frequency and wave length, enabling efficient problem solving despite significant variations in wave amplitude across different boundary layer thicknesses. A key aspect of smoothly varying materials is that even slight changes can result in substantial amplifications, potentially leading to non-linear effects that could potentially cause significant refraction. To analyze this, an adapted approximation is used that relates local and global frequency behaviors, providing a key insight that can lead to highly optimized mesh configurations, even those with significantly varying step sizes. While this approach does not utilize modern high-order approximation methods, it does yield highly accurate results, as verified through numerous test cases, including complex configurations with multiple objects and varied material properties, simulated both with adapting and fixed mesh configurations.

We analyzed the isotopic composition of oxygen and chromium within distinct grain populations within two recent meteorites: Chelyabinsk and Benenitra. Chelyabinsk allowed us to study grains that likely originated from a single fall event, whereas multiple fall events contributed to the analysis of Benenitra. Notably, Benenitra exhibited a more diverse range of isotopic compositions. Isotopic analysis of the 54-56 Cr ratio in Benenitra indicates a broader range of values, spanning from 0.0440 to 0.0447, which can be matched to five distinct components. In contrast, Chelyabinsk exhibited three of these components with similar ranges, from 0.0440 to 0.0445. The 17O and 18O isotopic analysis in both meteorites indicates a distinct offset, ranging from -0.001 to -0.002 in units relative to the CI chondrite in both cases. The data provide further support for previous research indicating that the inner Solar System experienced reduced accretion of planetesimals during the final stages of planetary formation, likely due to a decrease in dust availability. This theory is also consistent with the observed similarities between the isotopic composition of the terrestrial planets, including Earth. In this scenario, it is possible that the reduced accretion of planetesimals allowed the terrestrial planets to maintain a magnetic field, ultimately preventing a solar wind from stripping their atmospheres.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ models, including those with spin $s=2$, which correspond to the representation of the Lie algebra so(4) and are relevant to Heisenberg chains with SU(2)_q symmetries. We verify that both the quantum group symmetry and the Yang-Baxter equation are satisfied with specific quasi-homomorphism properties. Furthermore, we derive a novel algebraic expression for the form factors of one-particle states, which allows for a clear identification of the affine quantum-group symmetry and enables the comparison of Bethe-ansatz and algebraic construction methods.

Language barriers pose a significant challenge for effective communication, and the need for a swift and precise translation cannot be overstated. While significant progress has been made in both machine translation and speech recognition, little research has focused on combining these advancements for speech-to-text translation. This study aims to bridge this gap by proposing a novel approach called zero-shot voice translation, which leverages deep learning models incorporating speech recognition and advanced translation frameworks. We developed and evaluated a system combining a speech recognition model trained through transfer learning and a range of translation models, which demonstrated speech-to-text translation capabilities across multiple languages with minimal training. Notably, our findings showed that zero-shot learning translation achieved comparable performance to supervised learning translation between certain language pairs, such as English and French, but slightly underperformed. Conversely, zero-shot learning proved more effective for translating into languages with fewer spoken resources, such as Japanese and Korean.

We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic fields, encompassing both the static and dynamic aspects. We then demonstrate a novel approach to derive a comprehensive multipolar expansion, applicable to any phenomenon involving electromagnetic scattering and nonlinear responses, via a systematic approach involving linear and nonlinear algebra. This method is efficient, yielding a significant reduction in computational costs compared to conventional approaches. To showcase its effectiveness, we present a case study on the scattering patterns and optical force computations for dielectric particles in multiple scenarios and demonstrate that the proposed method is a more reliable and precise alternative to existing methods, even when the long wavelength approximation is violated.

This study delves into the properties and formation of quantum immanents for representations associated with the general linear Lie algebra. Our investigation focuses particularly on double Young-Capelli bitableaux and their implications within the context of Schur shifted symmetric functions. Key findings include: -The expression of specific double Young-Capelli bitableaux in terms of modified Mumford-Morrison elements, as well as their connection to extremal weight vectors. -A representation of elements from the Fock-Goncharov system of Lusztig parameters through double Young-Capelli bitableaux. -A method to derive elements of a certain subalgebra of the Yangian via Schur shifted symmetric functions from representations of the general linear Lie algebra. -Connections between certain double Young-Capelli bitableaux and elements of the Weyl algebra, also identifiable as quantum Schur positive elements.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the most basic variant involving two Higgs doublets and investigate its compatibility with the easiest "easy-SSM" scenario that maintains consistency with the electroweak precision data and dark matter properties. In the "easy-SSM" framework, the Higgs sector's vacuum stability is guaranteed, and a natural suppression of the Higgs natural parameter is achieved through the cancellation of the tree-level quartic Higgs self-interactions. Furthermore, this model modulates the dark matter relic density through a relevant interaction involving a scalar field associated with the electroweak symmetry breaking, allowing us to explore the phase space of a wide range of dark matter masses spanning from the sub-GeV regime to the several TeV range. In addition, a straightforward, efficient, and quasi-degenerate dark matter sector emerges, facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of a particular low-mass dark matter mass point that has been identified as a critical constraint. In this context, we establish the model's compliance with the WIMP (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles) paradigm by demonstrating that the model's dark matter mass fraction adheres to the $O(1)$ value as dictated by the ease-SSM scenario. A thorough analysis of the model's predictions and its implications for the LHC (Large Hadron Collider) and direct dark matter detection experiments has been performed.

We employ a versatile electronic structure model that distinguishes between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital character to examine the electronic properties of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal oxides. By utilizing a method that generalizes the Gutzwiller technique for correlated electrons, we calculate the spectral functions, effective masses, and carrier velocities for a range of these materials across different temperatures and doping levels. Our findings indicate a distinct response of the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ bands to electron-doping or temperature variation, which enables the disentanglement of their contributions to the transport phenomena. Notably, we observe that the $t_{2g}$ bands exhibit more significant electron-doping-induced widening compared to the $e_g$ bands, and display a more pronounced temperature dependence in some cases than the mass renormalization predicted by the conventional Fermi liquid theory. This distinction allows us to resolve the long-standing issue of the bimodal carrier velocity vs. density relation, and we establish a more general'velocity-doping curve' that is applicable across 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metal oxides.

Mirror symmetry implies that algebraic geometry has an equivalent'relative quantum geometry', which can be understood through the study of topological recursion. When considering Calabi-Yau manifolds that are in a certain relationship called 'birationally related', we can see that the knowledge of relative quantum geometry on one manifold allows us to deduce it on the other. In a significant breakthrough, we show that this relationship can be expressed in a more general way, which enables us to apply mirror symmetry to obtain insights into the geometry of certain 'families' of Calabi-Yau manifolds. This connection gives us a non-trivial equation that links the geometric properties of these manifolds. By looking at another aspect of mirror symmetry, known as 'landau-ginzburg', we can find solutions to this equation, which gives us a deeper understanding of the geometry of these manifolds.

The constant evolution of deep fake technology raises concerns about its potential to spread misinformation through manipulated medical images used to support false health claims. This study focuses on chest X-rays, a primary medical image type, by exploring the creation of realistic manipulations and the development of an effective detection system. A bespoke dataset was employed, comprising 5,000 images divided into training and testing sets. It was found that contemporary detection networks struggled to differentiate genuine and manipulated images but exhibited some ability to distinguish between different fabrication methods. Notably, a notable increase in detection accuracy was achieved by incorporating additional attributes into the classification, ultimately reaching 92% overall efficacy.

ViDaExpert is an innovative tool for multidimensional data visualization and advanced analysis. It empowers users to visualize high-dimensional data with unique features including variable dimensionality, orthogonal vectors, and distinct ball distributions. The tool allows for the exploration of data structures, including linear and nonlinear subspaces, and identifies patterns such as clusters within data sets. By simplifying complex high-dimensional data, ViDaExpert facilitates a deeper understanding and easier comparison of data sets. The software is available for download on the TOSCA website.

We have developed a highly efficient method for calculating potential fields and boundary values of integrals on two-dimensional domains, specifically those bounded by simple smooth curves. This method utilizes a localized approximation based on a combination of local polynomial and sinusoidal terms to represent the boundary. By taking into account boundary values of this combined series, we can accurately determine the harmonic field and derive a flexible and high-performance algorithm for solving boundary value problems and integral equations on such domains. Our code, readily available for download, demonstrates significant speed improvements over existing methods.
